edition.locus: Against Marcion 2.18 (talion restrains violence; food laws train; sacrifices curb idolatry)

source_text: Sed quae potius legis bona defendam quam quae haeresis concu(tel\'e concu)piit? ut talionis definitionem, oculum pro oculo dentem pro dente et liuorem pro liuore repetentis. non enim iniuriae mutuo exercendae licentiam sapit, sed in totum cohibendae uiolentiae prospicit, ut, quia durissimo et infideli in deum populo longum uel etiam incredibile uideretur a deo expectare defensam, edicendam postea per prophetam: mihi defensam, et ego defendam, dicit dominus, interim commissio iniuriae metu uicis statim occursurae repastinaretur et licentia retributionis prohibitio esset prouocationis. ut sic improbitas a se tuta cessaret, dum secunda permissa prima terretur et prima deterrita nec secunda committitur, qua et alias facilior timor talionis per eiusdem saporem passionis. nihil amarius quam id ipsum pati, quod feceris aliis. et si lex aliquid cibis detrahit et inmunda pronuntiat animalia, quae aliquando benedicta sunt, consilium exercendae continentiae intellege et frenos impositos illi gulae agnosce. quae, cum panem ederet angelorum, cucumeres et pepones Aegyptiorum + desiderabat. agnosce simul et comitibus gulae, libidini scilicet atque luxuriae, prospectum, quae fere uentris castigatione frigescunt; — manducauerat enim populus et biberat et surrexerat ludere — proinde, ut et pecuniae ardor restingeretur ex parte, qua de uictus necessitate causatur, pretiosorum ciborum ambitio detracta est; postremo, ut facilius homo ad ieiunandum deo formaretur, paucis et non gloriosis escis adsuefactus est. nihil de lautioribus esuriturus. reprehendendus sane creator, quod cibos potius populo suo abstulit quam ingratioribus Marcionitis. sacrificiorum quoque onera et operationum et oblationum negotiosas scrupulositates nemo reprehendat, quasi deus talia sibi proprie desiderauerit, qui tam manifeste exclamat: quo mihi multitudinem sacrificiorum uestrorum? et: quis exquisiuit ista de manibus uestris? sed illam dei industriam sentiat, qua populum pronum in idolatriam et transgressionem eiusmodi officiis religioni suae uoluit adstringere, quibus superstitio saeculi agebatur, ut ab ea auocaret illos, sibi iubens fieri, quasi desideranti, ne simulacris faciendo delinqueret.
pass_a_gloss: Talio cohibet uiolentiam. Cibi/sacrificia continentiam et ab idolis auocant.
pass_b_english: But which goods of the law shall I rather defend than those the heresy has struck at? As the definition of talion, demanding eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and bruise for bruise. For it does not savor a license of mutual injury to be practiced, but looks ahead to violence to be wholly restrained—so that, because to a people most hard and unbelieving toward God it seemed long or even incredible to expect defense from God, later to be declared through the prophet: Vengeance is mine, and I will avenge, says the Lord—meanwhile the committing of injury would be dug back by fear of a return about to meet at once, and license of repayment would be a prohibition of provocation.

Thus wickedness, safe from itself, would cease while the second permitted terrifies the first and the first deterred does not even commit the second—whereby also otherwise fear of talion is easier through the taste of the same passion. Nothing is more bitter than to suffer the very thing you have done to others. And if the law takes something away from foods and pronounces unclean animals that were once blessed, understand counsel of practicing continence and recognize bridles imposed on that gluttony which, when it was eating angels’ bread, was longing for Egypt’s cucumbers and melons. Recognize at the same time also provision for gluttony’s companions, namely lust and luxury, which nearly grow cold by chastisement of the belly—for the people had eaten and drunk and risen to play.

Likewise, that the heat of money might also be partly quenched, insofar as it is caused from necessity of living, ambition of precious foods was withdrawn; finally, that a human might more easily be formed to fasting for God, he was habituated to few and not glorious foods, about to hunger for nothing of the richer. The Creator is of course to be blamed because he rather took foods from his people than from more ungrateful Marcionites. Let no one also blame the burdens of sacrifices and the busy scrupulosities of works and offerings as if God properly desired such things for himself—who so openly cries: What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? and: Who sought these from your hands? But let him sense that industry of God by which he willed to bind a people prone to idolatry and transgression to his religion by such offices with which the age’s superstition was driven, so as to call them away from it, commanding them to be done for himself as if desiring, lest by doing for images they should sin.

what to me the multitude of sacrifices

choices.choice: read harsh law goods as pedagogy restraining violence, appetite, and idolatry
rejected: dismiss talion and food/sacrifice laws as unworthy of a good god

choices.choice: hear God’s rejection of sacrifice-hunger while keeping anti-idolatry industry
rejected: claim the Creator literally craved victims for himself
